steps.title: The missing bridge
paragraphs: Sam’s introduction went: “Have you ever seen a turtle eat a plastic bag? Cities should ban plastic bags.”
His friend read it and frowned. “Wait, why are turtles eating bags? How many bags are there?”
Sam added two sentences in the middle: “Turtles mistake floating bags for jellyfish, their favourite food. Every year, millions of bags blow from streets into rivers and the sea.”
Now the jump from turtles to the ban made sense. The middle sentences were a bridge from the hook to the thesis.

cards.title: What background does
cards.body: Background is one to three sentences between the hook and the thesis. It gives the reader what they need to understand your thesis: the situation, the problem, a key fact or a word to define. It moves from the hook (wide) to your thesis (narrow).

cards.title: Hook → background → thesis
cards.text:
Hook: Have you ever fallen asleep in first period?
Background: Most teenagers need about nine hours of sleep. But their body clocks make it hard to fall asleep before eleven, and many schools start before eight.
Thesis: Schools should start later because teens need more sleep, focus better when rested and are safer on the roads.
cards.note: The background explains the problem, so the thesis feels like the obvious answer.

cards.title: Not too much
cards.body: Background sets the scene; it doesn’t give your evidence away. Save your reasons, examples and quotes for the body paragraphs.

prompts: Read your hook and thesis without the background, then with it. What changes?
What does a reader need to know before your thesis makes sense?
